national.summary: Krakow police said a man who had driven onto the square began firing at random people from his car.
national.body: A man drove into an open market in the Polish city of Krakow and opened fire from his car, killing at least five people and injuring about a dozen others, police said. The shooter was shot by police and taken into custody, authorities said.The shooting happened in the Main Market Square in Krakow around 3 p.m. local time on Saturday. Krakow police said the alleged shooter began firing at random people from his car.Police officers are among the wounded. The perpetrator was shot and wounded during a confrontation with police and was taken to a hospital for treatment."I am being kept informed by the Minister of the Interior about the situation in Krakow following the tragic shooting," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrote on social media, adding that "the police are investigating the background and all the circumstances of the attack."Other details were not immediately available."We are just learning details of the horrific mass shooting in Krakow, a savage and murderous attack that's shattered the peace of Poland," Tom Rose, the U.S. ambassador to Poland, wrote on X. "America stands with Poland at this dark hour as Poland stands with her beloved citizens of Krakow."Krakow is the second-largest city in Poland and roughly 155 miles from the capital, Warsaw.

national.title: No clear winner after tight New Zealand general election
national.summary: Weeks of coalition talks could follow after preliminary results pointed to a highly divided national parliament.
national.body:
There was no clear winner following New Zealand's election on Saturday, as the leaders of its two major parties preparing for negotiations to form a coalition government.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's centre-right National Party won 42 seats but was 19 short of the simple majority needed to form a government, despite being the largest party, preliminary results show.

Combined with their coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First, they would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc if a deal could be reached.

But opposition leader Chris Hipkins, whose Labour Party won 36 seats, showed no signs of conceding, saying the "shape of the next government" will remain uncertain "for a while".

The tight result followed a campaign shaped by the cost of living and unemployment.

Projections show the National Party on 42 seats and Labour on 36. The Greens are on 16, with ACT on 13, New Zealand First on 12, the Opportunity Party on 7 and Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests, on 5.

The electoral commission was not due to announced the official result until 27 November.

Luxon congratulated Hipkins on a "very hard-fought race" before addressing party colleagues, saying "whatever the final count, we are incredibly proud of each and everyone for you".

national.title: U.S. expands naval blockade to include task force on disrupting ground transport
national.summary: The U.S. did not say whether any military action would be involved in preventing weapons technology or sanctioned items from entering Iran.
national.body: In what the U.S. military is calling an expansion of the naval blockade, U.S. Central Command announced a new task force Saturday aimed at disrupting the illegal shipment of prohibited items like military technology or illegal revenue streams over ground transportation routes. "The establishment of Task Force Iron Gate reinforces the success of our ironclad blockade against Iran at sea," U.S. Central Command chief Adm. Brad Cooper said in a statement. "Strengthening CENTCOM's collaboration with U.S. interagency partners will further constrain Iran's ability to finance terrorism, rebuild weapons factories, and replenish their military." The U.S. said the task force will be made up of about 20 civilian and military personnel, based in Florida, and will be tasked with the goal of "preventing the movement of advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials, and illegal revenue streams across Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea." The announcement made no mention of how the task force would be carrying out its goal, including whether any military operations will be involved. China, Iran's largest trade partner, has taken to conducting commerce over land, especially by train across central Asia due to the blockade on Iranian ports. The U.S. said the blockade has prevented some $25 billion in Iranian crude oil from being sold, much of it in Asia. In addition to China, Iran has conducted large amounts of trade over land and via the Caspian Sea with Russia. The landlocked Caspian Sea has proven especially advantageous with a direct route between southwest Russia and northern Iran. Tehran is located just 80 miles south of the Caspian Sea. Whether any U.S. ships could take to the Caspian Sea was again unclear. CBS News has reached out to the White House for more details.

national.title: A promising new medicine against heart disease fails unexpectedly
national.summary: Doctors expected an experimental drug that lowers a common risk factor for heart attacks would save patients' lives. The medicine made no difference.
national.body:
An experimental drug doctors hoped would be the next big advance in preventing heart attacks and strokes failed a crucial test, researchers reported Saturday.

Living Better Heart disease deaths declined. And here's how to reduce your risk of the #1 killer The medicine, which reduces levels of a particle in the blood associated with heart attacks and strokes, didn't protect volunteers in a closely watched study.

"I was shocked. I had high hopes for success," says Steven Nissen , a cardiologist at the Cleveland Clinic who led the study. "Cardiovascular disease is still the leading cause of death in developed countries. And so we really were hoping to find additional therapies that would reduce risk."

The research aimed to help people who seem to do everything right. They keep their cholesterol and blood pressure low, eat well, maintain a healthy weight, and exercise regularly. But many still suffer heart attacks and strokes.

"That sort of patient we see very frequently, and we were really doing our best to try to find a way to help those patients," Nissen says.

Many of these patients have elevated blood levels of a cholesterol-carrying protein called lipoprotein(a) or Lp(a), which has long been thought to increase the risk for heart disease.

"About 20% of the global population have elevated levels. And that's about a billion people. So it's a common disorder," Nissen says.

Until recently, doctors didn't have any drugs that could lower Lp(a) levels. But several drug companies have developed experimental new medications in recent years that can slash elevated Lp(a).

national.summary: Top Trump adviser Stephen Miller, who is set to take over the White House chief of staff role on Monday, has driven President Trump's most controversial immigration policies during both of his administrations.
national.body: Washington — Top Trump adviser Stephen Miller, who is set to take over the White House chief of staff role on Monday, has driven President Trump's most controversial immigration policies during both of his administrations. Mr. Trump announced the staffing shake-up on Friday, calling Miller one of his "most trusted" advisers. Miller replaces Susie Wiles, who has been his chief of staff throughout his second term. The move comes after Republicans suffered crippling losses in the midterm elections and as Democrats plan sweeping investigations into the administration's actions, including its immigration enforcement policies. Miller was the architect behind many of those policies and also championed the administration's immigration enforcement expansion, which has been supported by approximately $170 billion that congressional Republicans allocated for immigration enforcement and border security in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which became law in July 2025. During Mr. Trump's first term, Miller helped develop and publicly defend the administration's executive order that restricted entry by nationals of several Muslim-majority countries. The travel ban led to protests around the U.S. and legal challenges. A third iteration of the ban was upheld by the Supreme Court in 2018. He was a leading supporter of the administration's 2018 zero-tolerance immigration policy, which resulted in thousands of family separations, and he pressed for dramatic reductions in refugee admissions. The administration repeatedly lowered the annual refugee admissions ceiling, ultimately setting it at 15,000 for fiscal year 2021, a record low at the time. Under former President Barack Obama, the ceiling was 110,000 for fiscal year 2017. Miller also advocated penalizing legal immigrants who received public benefits and making it harder for them to obtain citizenship. In Mr. Trump's second term, Miller pushed Immigration and Customs Enforcement to make at least 3,000 immigration arrests per day. In May 2025, Miller publicly demanded a dramatic increase in daily arrests, placing pressure on ICE leadership and expanding enforcement beyond immigrants who had been convicted of serious crimes. He also proposed that the National Guard be deployed to support mass deportations. national.title: Democrats plan to widen their probes of fatal ICE shootings
national.summary: The killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti during the ICE surge in Minneapolis last winter was a pivotal moment for the country. After Democrats' sweeping wins this week, their deaths at the hands of immigration agents will likely be the targets of renewed investigations.
national.body:
The morning after Tuesday's midterms was gloomy and rainy in Minneapolis, but people still gathered at the place where Border Patrol agents shot and killed Alex Pretti, a VA nurse and U.S. citizen, last January. All week, community members have come here to place their "I Voted" stickers at the memorial.

Nicki Adams, who dated Pretti and was his close friend for nearly 17 years, watched quietly as a woman added her sticker to a street lamp completely covered in the red decals.

"I wanted to see all the stickers. I just wanted to be here," she says. "It just means a lot to me. I think it would mean a lot to Alex, too."

A few blocks away, people left their stickers where an ICE officer killed Renee Good, a mom of three and a U.S. citizen, just a few weeks before Pretti's death. In Houston, they left them where an ICE officer killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a father of three and a Mexican immigrant, in July.

Adams says these stickers, and the election results this week, send a clear message to Congress: "You work for us, and please carry on these values that we care about … We want to be seen and heard and taken care of and have our neighbors taken care of."

The deaths of Pretti and Good during the ICE surge in Minneapolis marked a pivotal moment for the country, sparking intense public backlash to President Trump's aggressive deportation efforts. But federal law enforcement officials have given little indication they're progressing in investigating their deaths, or the deaths of at least seven other people killed by federal immigration agents since Trump took office again last year. DHS did not respond to an NPR request for the status of those investigations.

Now, after Democrats' sweeping wins this week, their deaths at the hands of immigration agents will likely be the targets of renewed investigations. With a majority in Congress, Democrats can issue subpoenas to the major players in Trump's mass deportation plan, compelling them to testify under oath before the legislature.

That could include White House Border Czar Tom Homan, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, former Border Patrol Commander Gregory Bovino, and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, among others.

national.title: No one knew why a dad couldn't eat. Then a surgeon took a second look.
national.summary: Richard Satin was in constant pain and couldn't eat. He was sure he was dying — until a surgeon found something unusual.
national.body: Richard Satin was sure he was dying. Things had been fine until the fall of 2025. He had enjoyed the summer with his wife and 8-year-old daughter, including taking a trip to Disney. But in October, he woke up in the middle of the night in agony. When his wife, Farrah, rushed him to a Long Island hospital, tests showed his blood sugar was spiking. Doctors found he had developed diabetes. They also identified a blood clot in his portal vein, which connects the gastrointestinal tract to the liver. They treated the clot and stabilized his diabetes. He was discharged a week later with the new diagnosis. But it was the start of a vicious cycle. Within days, Satin was in pain again and returned to the hospital. Doctors had few answers. During one visit, a doctor recommended a high-fiber diet. Another visit came with a recommendation for a liquid diet. Nothing helped. Soon, Satin lost all appetite. Eating a bowl of Jell-O became an achievement. His daughter became frightened by his appearance. His favorite hobby, golf, was impossible. By mid-December, he had lost 70 pounds. His wife was at the end of her rope. "Farrah just looked at me and said 'We can't go down this path anymore. We've got to do something,'" Satin recalled. The couple began reaching out to specialists, but many weren't available for months. Satin, convinced he wouldn't make it that long, made an appointment with a concierge doctor, Dr. William Klein. On Christmas Eve, he had his first appointment with Klein. "He examined me for a couple of hours, took lots of vials of blood, and said, 'If you don't have surgery immediately, you are in trouble,'" Satin said. A life-saving surgery Klein determined that Satin had an issue in his gastrointestinal tract, but was stumped on exactly what was wrong. He referred Satin to a surgeon, Dr. Gary Gecelter, chairman of the Department of Surgery at St. Francis Hospital & Heart Center. national.title: Russian strikes wound nine and damage Ukraine's power network ahead of talks
national.summary: The attacks come before Ukrainian and Russian delegations are due to take part in trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi next week.
national.body:
Overnight drone and ballistic missile attacks damaged Ukrainian energy infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskyhas said, causing blackouts and disrupting water supplies.

Zelensky said 12 Ukrainian regions came under attack with the capital Kyiv hit hardest.

Nine people are reported to have been hurt across the country, including one child, in the wave of attacks that consisted of more than 30 ballistic missiles and over 170 drones.

The attacks come before Ukrainian and Russian delegations are due to take part in trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi next week.

Zelensky wrote on Telegram , external that Moscow was preparing for the talks by launching attacks on Ukraine's "critical infrastructure".

Temperatures are dropping in Ukraine, and parts of the country have had the first winter snow.

"The situation in the capital is difficult, with disruptions to electricity, water, and heating supplies. Residential buildings, the North Bridge, and a kindergarten have been damaged," Zelensky said.

"In the Kyiv region, there were strikes on substations that connect the Rivne and Khmelnytsky nuclear power plants to Kyiv and central Ukraine."

Buoyed by major gains in Congress, Democrats will have momentum as they prepare for the contest to succeed President Donald Trump.

But a good showing in the midterms does not guarantee a White House win two years later. Barack Obama was re-elected in 2012 despite huge Republican gains in 2010.

No one has yet entered the presidential race but potential candidates will be preparing behind the scenes.

Vice-President's JD Vance's reflection on where the midterms went wrong for Republicans has been interpreted as him paving the way for a 2028 run.

The results of Tuesday's election and the historic size of Democratic gains could shape the White House race in several ways. Here are four takeaways.

Several prominent potential presidential candidates were running in the 2026 midterms - and some emerged looking strong.

No one has yet entered the presidential race but potential candidates will be preparing behind the scenes.

national.title: This teen boy set out to get people talking about periods. He's now a Diana honoree
national.summary: This year's the Princess Diana honor roll highlights 198 inspiring young activists and advocates — including an 18-year-old guy in India who founded Team Period.
national.body:
Aadvik Jain (third from right) has won a Princess Diana award for starting Team Period to counter menstrual stigma. He's standing with other members of this activist group and teacher Sonia Rao (center, in green sari). "Our work would not be possible without her guidance and support," he says. Team Period hide caption

Can a teenage boy change the way people think about menstruation?

At just 14, Aadvik Jain, studying in India's capital city, Delhi, set out to do exactly that. It all began when he had to watch a close friend struggle with debilitating menstrual pain that wasn't being taken seriously.

This year, he's among the 198 young people from 44 countries who were honored with the Diana Award, an international recognition for young changemakers working to improve lives in their communities. The awardees were announced on November 4 at a virtual ceremony streamed internationally.

Established in memory of Diana, Princess of Wales, the international award recognizes young people ages 16 to 25 for their social action and humanitarian efforts. This year, India accounted for nearly a quarter of the recipients, with 49 honorees.

Among them are Shiv Mandlik, who invented a bendable pole to help construction workers avoid working at dangerous heights and who developed an app to detect falls; Krish Aggarwal, who created an inexpensive filter that can be fitted onto ordinary fans to reduce indoor air pollution; and Kushal Sachdeva, who at age 11 began feeding a starving street dog. His organization, Protect Paws, has reportedly helped more than 1,500 stray dogs by arranging for medical treatment, vaccinations and reflective collars.

And then there's Jain. Now 18, he leads Team Period, an initiative he started in 2024 with three close friends. Together, they are challenging menstrual stigma through workshops, street performances, awareness campaigns and efforts to improve access to menstrual pads and products. He's also set to start studying medicine and public health at the University of Bologna in Italy in February.

Aadvik Jain, founder of Team Period, plans to study medicine and public health in Italy next year. Team Period hide caption

national.title: Paraguay's president under house arrested after bank collapse
national.summary: The president was placed under house arrest after being removed from office following the collapse of a bank linked to the government.
national.body: Paraguay's president has been placed on house arrest on Friday after the collapse of a government-linked bank that locked nearly half the country's population out of their accounts.Paraguay's Senate voted to remove Santiago Peña for misconduct in office, making him the second president ousted by impeachment since the end of Gen. Alfredo Stroessner's 35-year dictatorship in 1989.Regulators had seized Ueno Bank just three days earlier, sending shock waves through the financial system and setting off the country's worst political crisis in more than a decade.Peña was ordered to remain at one of his homes in Asunción until he appears before prosecutors Saturday morning on charges of breach of trust, influence peddling and using public office for personal gain, the most serious of which carry up to 10 years in prison. Lawmakers accuse him of using his political influence to steer hundreds of millions of dollars in public funds into Ueno while regulators overlooked risky insider lending.The Paraguayan president denied wrongdoing.When regulators seized the bank, Ueno customers could no longer withdraw cash, access their savings or use their cards to buy anything. The digital lender had aggressively courted the poor and unbanked with generous supermarket rebates, and more than 1 million Paraguayans opened their first bank account there, according to Ueno. Even players on the national soccer team, which Ueno sponsored through its run to a World Cup upset of Germany this year, say they can't reach their money.The fallout has spread well beyond savers. A ride-hailing app that relied on Ueno shut down, leaving 3,000 drivers without work. The state power company says $21 million in loans from the Inter-American Development Bank and Taiwan, earmarked for public works, is trapped at the bank. Paraguay's bonds have posted some of the worst losses in emerging markets this week, and the guaraní has slid against the dollar.Some depositors began recovering their money Thursday, starting with those holding up to 10 million guaraníes (about $1,500). Deposits are insured up to about $35,000, which the central bank says covers 97% of Ueno's customers. It calls the collapse an isolated case and insists the broader financial system is safe.

national.title: An unexpected activist emerged to help block a $5 billion data center in Maryland
national.summary: Thousands across the U.S. have gotten involved to oppose data centers. One is a Maryland woman who'd been evicted after a pay cut and became a leader of a community effort that blocked a vast project.
national.body:
Taylor Frazier McCollum has been active in the opposition to the possible data center at the site of the demolished Landover Mall in Prince George's County, less than a mile from where she lived. If the project is built, the development could occupy more than 80 acres. Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR hide caption

The overgrown grass and weeds seem to stretch into the horizon on nearly 90 acres of empty land in Landover, Md. It used to be Landover Mall, but that closed in 2002, and the site has been mostly vacant since.

In 2024, the developer that built the mall won approval from county planners for a $5 billion data center campus, and word began spreading through the largely Black community nearby.

"I was like, 'Oh, hell no,'" said Taylor Frazier McCollum, describing the moment she learned about the project. She lived less than a mile away from it. "Why would you want to bring water-polluting, diesel-generating data centers right down the street from where people live, work, play? It just didn't make sense to me."

Frazier McCollum is one of a number of Americans whose political awakening was triggered by data center development. Across the country, community members have taken to local council hearings to voice their opposition. They've prompted — though estimates vary — about 500 moratoriums on data centers nationwide.

Unlike a lot of land-use activists trying to protect their homes from threats in their backyards, Frazier McCollum does not own a home. In 2024, she and her young daughter were evicted from their apartment. She was working at a waxing center that cut wages, and she could no longer cover her rent.

"It was difficult," Frazier McCollum recalled. "Because I created the ideal life paying for us to live in this apartment and have our own space ... and then to have it taken away ... It felt like something that wasn't ever going to end."

They've moved around and were living in her grandfather's home when she learned about the proposed project less than a mile away.

national.title: Texas mayor instructs police to limit co-operation with ICE
national.summary: There has been months of public outcry in Houston after an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer fatally shot a man who was driving to work.
national.body:
The mayor of Houston, Texas, has directed the city's police to limit co-operation with federal immigration officials.

The move by John Whitmire, a Democrat, comes on the heels of stunning victories by the party in Texas during this week's midterm elections. It breaks with policy set by Republican Governor Greg Abbott, who lost his re-election bid.

"I do this to begin a healing process," Whitmire said on Friday, and to "reduce fear and anxiety across our community". He added: "I also do this knowing that elections matter."

There has been months of public outcry in Houston after an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer fatally shot a man who was driving to work.

Houston police chief Noe Diaz said on Friday that officers will now only contact ICE if someone they arrest for a jailable offence also has an administrative ICE warrant, which are issued internally by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), within which ICE operates.

"For example, if our police officers pull someone over for a minor traffic infraction and they write a citation, that person receives a citation and goes about their day," Diaz said.

Under the previous rules, Houston police officers were required to inform ICE if anyone they were dealing with came up as having one of these warrants attached to their name when they were searched on the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) - a digital database that includes records on wanted persons, stolen property, certain missing people and those arrested and fingerprinted for serious offences.

Whitmire said on Friday that he had directed the Houston Police Department to make the changes through an executive order.

national.title: Meghan's father Thomas Markle under house arrest after child sex abuse material charge
national.summary: The 82-year-old appeared in court in Florida after the FBI searched two Los Angeles-area storage units he rented.
national.body:
Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, has been placed under house detention at his assisted living facility in Florida after being charged over possession of child sex abuse material.

Markle, 82, was arrested in Florida on a federal complaint alleging he held images that show child sex abuse, the US Department of Justice (DoJ) said.

He is charged with one count of possessing indecent images of children, the DoJ said. Markle has previously denied allegations of possessing images of child sex abuse, calling them "sick lies".

In a 30-minute court hearing on Friday he was also ordered to submit to electronic monitoring, but no plea was taken.

At the court hearing, the charges were laid out against him by federal prosecutor Courtenay Derry, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News.

He was brought into court in a wheelchair, escorted by two US Marshals. Markle was wearing black trousers and a black t-shirt.

No plea was taken during the hearing, and an arraignment date in California will be determined in due course, a joint statement from the DoJ and the US Attorney's Office Central California said.

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have not commented on Markle's arrest.

national.title: Paraguay's president impeached and under house arrest after bank collapse
national.summary: Santiago Peña was ousted due to a banking crisis which left millions of people unable to access their money.
national.body:
Paraguay's President Santiago Peña has been impeached and placed under house arrest after a bank collapse triggered a crisis that left more than half of the country's population without access to their accounts.

Peña was arrested on Friday minutes after lawmakers, including from his own party, unanimously voted to remove him from office following the collapse earlier this week of Ueno Bank, which has links to his private business interests.

He had offered to step down on Thursday. Rather than accept his resignation, senators impeached Peña and charged him with misconduct, meaning he has been stripped of the immunity usually granted to ex-presidents.

Peña, who until last year held shares in the company that owned the bank, has denied any wrongdoing.

The impeachment charges that led to Peña's removal alleged he had conflicts of interest, manipulated regulatory oversight, diverted pension funds, and participated in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank.

He is due to be questioned on Saturday over allegations of breach of trust, influence peddling, and misappropriation of funds, prosecutor Silvia Margarita Gonzalez Vester said.

Peña's deputy, Pedro Alliana, has been sworn in as the new interim president and promised not to "abandon" the millions of people affected by the scandal.

"Compatriots who are now going through a difficult time as a result of the financial collapse will be fully compensated," said Alliana, who will serve as president until 2028.

national.title: Pope in 'pretty good health' as he starts Latin America tour
national.summary: Pope Leo travels to Uruguay just three weeks after having surgery for lung cancer.
national.body:
Pope Leo XIV has told reporters travelling with him to Latin America he is "in pretty good health", in his first comments on his condition since having surgery for lung cancer.

The Pope has arrived in Uruguay, the first stop of a 12-day tour which he is undertaking only three weeks after his operation.

The pontiff, 71, also said he was "very happy" to be able to make the trip which was thrown into doubt last month when doctors discovered a tumour during a routine scan.

The tour will cover Argentina and a much anticipated return to Peru , which the Vatican described as a "homecoming" as the Pope was based there for many years as a missionary, then a bishop.

"I must confess that, from the very first day, I never had any doubts; I was convinced that this journey had to go forward," the Pope told journalists on his plane to Uruguay.

"Thanks to the marvellous medical staff... I believe I am in quite good health," Pope Leo confirmed.

Last month's operation to remove a tumour was successful and his doctors say the cancer has not spread.

On Friday, he arrived in Monetevideo to a seafront lined with crowds shouting his name as his Popemobile passed.

national.title: How 2 lifelong singles in the same town ended up married
national.summary: Al Sager, 65, and Susan Guc, 76, had both been happily single for decades. Then they met in the most surprising way, and everything changed.
national.body: For his entire life, 65-year-old Al Sager of Bay City, Michigan, had been single."You see relationships sour and it's like, 'Nah, I don't want that,'" Sager told CBS News. "â¦ I was alone, but I wasn't lonely." Across town, meanwhile, 76-year-old Susan Guc felt the same. "If there would be anybody out there, who would I really want?" Guc said. As it turned out, the answer was nobody. "And I was happy with that," she said. "I really was."Guc worked as a nurse devoted solely to her patients. Sager was a truck driver who was always on the road. They were two of Bay City's most committed "uncommitteds."Until this week, when they were married. All those years of singlehood came to a surprising end, leaving relatives in disbelief."We were all just shocked," one relative said. "I about fell out of my chair," said another. "I didn't expect that." Guc explained: "It was just a fluke."It all began a couple of years ago, according to Guc, when they both underwent heart procedures and were placed in the same cardiac rehab program.Guc was on a treadmill when she noticed Sager on an exercise bike. He didn't notice anything, but she really liked his smile.He was oblivious to her, so she hit him with a rock â literally. The rock had the word "smile" etched on it. "Yes, she threw a rock at me to get my attention," Sager said. "This rock rocked," Guc said.Actually, she more like handed it to him, but it did knock him for a loop. "I thought she was trying to tell me, 'Hey, you don't smile enough,'" Sager said. "â¦ And I said, 'Well, I better look into this more.'"Today, Sager and Guc are all smiles and beaming a message to anyone out there who thinks they're too old to find their person."I had thought that, but look what happened to me," Guc said. Added Sager, "Oh, absolutely, it's never too late."

national.body: The Justice Department on Friday moved to dismiss its own lawsuit that sought to stop California from counting roughly 20,000 ballots it alleged went to noncitizens until their immigration status could be verified.The request to dismiss the case comes days after Republicans' significant losses in the midterm elections and about a week before a scheduled hearing where a special master was slated to evaluate the accuracy of the list. national.summary: Secret Service officers found three weapons in the vehicle of the suspect, who allegedly told officers he had heard voices in his head telling him to come to Washington and assassinate the president.
national.body: An undocumented immigrant armed with several weapons was taken into custody within blocks of the White House Thursday night after he allegedly told Secret Service officers that he was planning an attempt on President Trump's life, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security said.The suspect, identified as Ronny Yordrix Guanipa Chrinos of Venezuela, was arrested on three counts each of unlawful transportation of a firearm, carrying unregistered firearms and carrying unregistered ammunition, along with one count each of possession of certain dangerous weapons, carrying a pistol without a license, unauthorized use of a motor vehicle, theft and receiving stolen property, DHS said in a news release Friday. Secret Service officers observed the suspect acting suspiciously in his vehicle and approached him while he was parked on Constitution Avenue, DHS said. The Secret Service officers learned the suspect's vehicle had been reported stolen, DHS said, and the suspect allegedly admitted there were weapons in the vehicle. When officers searched the vehicle, they found three firearms, including a rifle, as well as dozens of rounds of ammunition, according to DHS, which released a photo of the seized items. national.title: This man refused life-saving treatment because of his religion - days later the rules changed
national.summary: Jehovah's Witness leaders relaxed strict rules on blood transfusions, but the change came 23 days too late for Isaac Valdez.
national.body:
In August this year, 26-year-old Isaac Valdez had an epileptic seizure while browsing in his local library, causing him to convulse and strike his head against the ground.

He lost consciousness. Later, in hospital, it transpired Isaac had hit his head with such force it had led to a brain haemorrhage.

Treatment was seriously complicated by the fact that, as a Jehovah's Witness, Isaac carried a "No Blood" card, an indication that he would not accept treatment involving any form of blood transfusion because of his religious beliefs.

As a result, a procedure to drain fluid from Isaac's brain did not take place.

But his family, from Waxahachie, Texas, were encouraged by the fact that he regained consciousness and even started to talk again. He was able to confirm that he stood by his "no blood" beliefs.

The family's relief at his apparent improvement was short-lived. Isaac slipped into a coma and his condition worsened rapidly.

A neurosurgeon told Isaac's family the only way to save his life was an emergency operation, but that it was one that required blood transfusion.

His family took the decision to abide by Issac's wishes as a lifelong Witness not to accept such a procedure.

national.title: The young Somali woman changing how the world sees Mogadishu
national.summary: For some tourists, the contrast between Somalia's reputation and what they experience on the ground can be striking.
national.body:
As the sun rises over the Indian Ocean, waves lap onto the golden sands while palm fronds rustle in the cool sea breeze. Welcome to... Mogadishu.

This is the image that one young Somali woman wants the world to have of her home city - in contrast to the one of suicide attacks and young men wielding AK-47s that many people currently associate with Somalia's capital.

Sucdi Abdul Fattah Abdul Khader is among a growing number of local guides taking visitors beyond the headlines to explore Mogadishu's beauty spots, historic sites and culture.

Her favourite spot is Jazeera beach, where visitors can enjoy the sea before heading to nearby sand dunes.

"It's one of the tourist attractions where we bring our guests. It's a nice place," says the 23-year-old.

national.title: Cornell faculty pass no-confidence vote over leadership's handling of Jane Doe allegations
national.summary: Friday's resolution by academic staff is largely symbolic as they do not have the power to remove those in charge of the university.
national.body:
Cornell University's academic staff have passed a vote of no confidence over its leadership's handling of what staff call a "crisis of sexual assault" after a former student alleged she was gang raped while attending.

The woman, known anonymously as Jane Doe, is suing her former university and the fraternity over an alleged incident involving several men at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024.

All seven of the accused have denied wrongdoing when contacted by the BBC's US partner CBS. None has been charged with a crime.

Friday's no-confidence vote passed by 75 votes to 50. It is largely symbolic because the faculty senate does not have the power to remove leaders.

The resolution states that the faculty senate, which represents academic staff, "has no confidence in the ability of the central administration to effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault at Cornell University".

It did not make any specific recommendations or suggest what administrators did wrong in response to the accusation.

It is a rebuke of university leaders including President Michael Kotlikoff, whom Doe has accused of asking why she waited several weeks to report the incident.

The Ivy League institution in upstate New York has said her account of Kotlikoff's reaction is "incorrect".

local.body:
FALCONER -- Chautauqua Lake/Westfield/Brocton's offense has been a work in progress all season.

That unit is taking the Eagles to the Section VI Class C final.

Chautauqua Lake/Westfield/Brocton, Class C South's No. 3 seed, allowed just 68 yards rushing and stopped both of Falconer/Cassadaga Valley/Maple Grove's trips inside the red zone to beat the Herd 14-0 in a semifinal Friday night at Bill Race Field.

"It was pretty evident early on in the season that defensively we were going to be pretty tough. ... If we're being honest, the defense has really carried us for the better part of the season. (Chris) Payne has done a tremendous job as always," Harper said of his longtime defensive coordinator. "You can count on it: death, taxes and Chris Payne's defense."

The win sends the defending sectional champions into next Friday's 2 p.m. title game against Barker/Royalton-Hartland at the University at Buffalo's Broadview Stadium. The Bulls, Class C North's top seed, beat Clymer/Sherman/Panama 24-20 in Friday's other semifinal.

"They are big. They are physical. They have a great back," Harper said of Barker/Royalton-Hartland. "They don't really do anything fancy. They get into a stack-I and they are going to run the ball right at you. That's tough to stop."

Chautauqua Lake/Westfield/Brocton didn't shine offensively in Falconer -- Tristen Gibbs led the Eagles with 21 carries for 109 yards -- but the Eagles did force three turnovers and stop Falconer/Cassadaga Valley/Maple Grove on downs three other times.

"Chris Payne did a great job. If there was a Player of the Game, it would have been Chris Payne for preparing them really well," Falconer/Cassadaga Valley/Maple Grove head coach Curt Fischer said. "He's a great coach and I have a lot of respect for him."

JAMESTOWN -- Cornell Cooperative Extension Chautauqua County's 4-H Program is asking the community for donations for our inaugural Handmade for the Holidays Event.

Handmade for the Holidays will be held on Dec. 5 at the JCC Carnahan Center on the JCC Campus (241 James Ave, Jamestown). This open-house style event will run from 10:00 a.m. - 3:00 p.m. This event is cash only and admission costs $8 per person with a family cap of $40. Soup lunch, hot beverages, craft kits, and a "fill your own craft supply bag" will be available for purchase at the event.

Participants will have the opportunity to move between 8 crafting stations making handmade gifts to take home. With crafts like needle felted wool ornaments, custom Epsom salt soaks, and a custom-made cardboard winter scene, there is something for everyone on your list.

The Chautauqua County 4-H Program is one of many programs offered by Cornell Cooperative Extension of Chautauqua County (CCE-Chautauqua). CCE-Chautauqua is a subordinate governmental agency with an educational mission that operates under a form of organization and administration approved by Cornell University as agent for the State of New York. It is tax-exempt under section 501(c)(3) of the Internal Revenue Code. The association is part of the national cooperative extension system, an educational partnership between County, State, and Federal governments.

As New York's land grant university Cornell administers the system in this state. Each Cornell Cooperative Extension association is an independent employer that is governed by an elected Board of Directors with general oversight from Cornell. All associations work to meet the needs of the counties in which they are located as well as state and national goals. For more information, call 716-664-9502 or visit our website at www.cce.cornell.edu/chautauqua. Cornell University Cooperative Extension provides equal program and employment opportunities.

local.title: Dunkirk chief offers reassurance on BESS
local.summary: Battery Energy Storage Systems do offer unique hazards, Dunkirk Fire Chief Nicholas Barter said last week. However, as he pointed out, “Everything has risk — everything we do.” BESS discussion was the highlight of a talk Barter gave to Revitalize Dunkirk’s quarterly meeting. “At some point, it’s goi
local.body:
Battery Energy Storage Systems do offer unique hazards, Dunkirk Fire Chief Nicholas Barter said last week. However, as he pointed out, "Everything has risk -- everything we do."

BESS discussion was the highlight of a talk Barter gave to Revitalize Dunkirk's quarterly meeting.

"At some point, it's going to be here," he said. "I'm going to recognize that for what it is, at the scale of a community and a hazard we have to plan for."

The systems store varying amounts of power from the electric grid, for release in times of high demand. "We've been working with developers because we have concerns as well," Barter said.

"There is definitely a risk with them -- but it is projected to everyone's mind by high profile incidents," he said. Barter mentioned a major January 2025 fire in Moss Landing, California, that prompted evacuations. The fire briefly rekindled in September during cleanup operations.

However, he noted, every BESS is different -- and part of what led to and worsened the Moss Landing fire was the enclosure of storage arrays in a concrete building. The two BESS proposals for Dunkirk would be open-air. One of the proposals is approved for currently unused land several hundred yards from Brigham Road, another is sought closer to the same road but not approved.

Barter said his department will approach open-air BESS fires with the attitude of, "It's almost let it burn."

He acknowledged that is an unusual tactic, but said it is occasionally used with chemical fires. "It does sound bad, but there is a plan out there."

local.title: Voters took control of misguided U.S. leadership
local.summary: What an election! Folks, the power has always been ours, we just need to be convinced to use it! local.body:
What an election! Folks, the power has always been ours, we just need to be convinced to use it! For every election, large or small, we should have a very modest expectation that at least a majority of registered voters would cast a ballot. I heard so many folks at the polls say this, that if you don't vote, don't complain. These people take their responsibility seriously, as we all should.

Not every country affords its citizens the right and privilege of a say in its government, and we are lucky to be where we are, and to be part of this blue wave that is rising to the occasion. This nation was founded on the principles of government of, by, and for, the people. Without the "by" there isn't a "for" for long. We must not take that responsibility lightly.

Up until Tuesday, our future as a democratic country was in jeopardy. Tuesday's election results grabbed us back from the precipice of autocracy - for now. But it shouldn't have taken this long, so much damage has been done to our beloved country and its citizens, so much greed, corruption, hatred, ignoring of the common good of the people.

The plan to take the reins of government away from the people and give them to the huge corporate CEOs, to put big business interests in charge of us, to make us feudal peasants to the moneyed class, was taken from the pages of history and put into the pages of Project 2025. If we can build on the momentum that this election has given us, we may see this plan unravel. Trump was useful to the Project while things were going well, now they may not be too happy with him either. We may see rats jumping ship. We may see Elon go try to ply his influence elsewhere. We can only hope. We the people must stay strong.

Remember, our votes are what puts the politicians where they are. If we just let them go their merry way without holding them accountable to us, how many of them will stay true to their campaign promises? Very few. It takes strong character, an internal honesty and integrity, and if that is not something they have carried with them since their childhood, it is very easy for them to make excuses and to follow the shiny objects of wealth and power. We have to keep them in line, be strict parents, and we have not been doing a good job lately. They need to know we are paying attention.

For instance, just a factual five-minute biography read on DJT would have told every voter all they needed to know about his real-life history and why to avoid electing him at all costs. But so many chose not to take the time, to listen to his snake-oil pitch (remember the story about the snake he always liked to tell - that was him revealing his truth, just as clear as day), and believe his made-up reality showbiz persona. It was so much more fun to go to his rallies, to laugh at his nonsense, to feel authenticated in the grievances that he assured his followers were the fault of Obama, or Biden, or their next-door neighbor- anything to take away the pain of responsibility rather than work toward a way to fix them. We all were warned, now we have to claw our way back from the ruination that he inevitably caused, – that was predicted by everything he has done his entire life.

OBSERVER Photo by Jon Neubauer Silver Creek/Forestville's Dom Anders catches a touchdown from Will Duliba over the head of Newfane defender Levi Henning during the Section VI Class D semifinals on Friday night.

OBSERVER Photo by Jon Neubauer Silver Creek/Forestville's Manny Sanchez looks for room to run after receiving the handoff from quarterback Will Duliba during the Section VI Class D semifinals at Newfane on Friday night.

NEWFANE -- Less than six minutes into its semifinal matchup at No. 2 Newfane, the Silver Creek/Forestville football team was already down by two scores. The 3-seeded Black Knights chased the defending-champion Panthers all game and Newfane raced to a 44-20 victory in the Section VI Class D semifinals on Friday night.

The opening kickoff spelled doom for the Black Knights as a line drive kick could not be handled and Newfane recovered to score only three plays later when Nasir Spencer broke free for a 20-yard touchdown.

Trailing 8-0 early, Silver Creek/Forestville did not have much of an answer when it did receive the following kickoff as it went three and out. Newfane then promptly worked into Silver Creek/Forestville territory and Spencer rattled off a 19-yard run to put the Panthers up 14-0.

Silver Creek/Forestville was down, but certainly not out as it showed on the next drive. Working with a short field, Manny Sanchez made it even shorter when he broke off a 45-yard run down to the Newfane 10.

The Panthers would not allow the Black Knights to reach the end zone easily as it was 4th-and-5 when Will Duliba rolled out on the play-action pass to find Dom Anders for the 5-yard touchdown pass. Anders followed up catching the two-point conversion and Silver Creek/Forestville had something to build on.

While the offense found its footing, the Silver Creek/Forestville defense could not stop the Newfane attack and the Panthers finally ran some time off the clock on a drive which they eventually finished in the second quarter. Instead of Spencer on the ground, quarterback Jesse Hughey connected with Mikey Henning for a 27-yard touchdown pass and Jake Morello's run made it a 22-8 score.

Submitted Photos The annual Empty Bowls fundraiser in Fredonia is set for Nov. 21. Pictured is the crowd at last year’s Empty Bowls event at the Wheelock School in Fredonia.

Pictured is Layla Gallaway, a Fredonia student, with a custom bowl at last year’s Empty Bowls fundraiser in Fredonia.

Later this month, one of the area's most impactful fundraisers each year will give patrons a chance to fill their cupboards while also stocking the shelves of food pantries across the county.

The annual Empty Bowls fundraiser will be held on Saturday, Nov. 21, beginning at 11 a.m. until 2 p.m., at Fredonia's Wheelock School gymnasium. Approximately 1,000 custom bowls will be available for purchase at Wheelock, with proceeds to be donated to combat food insecurity in the community through local food pantries supported by FeedMore WNY.

Roughly a dozen professional artists have designed bowls of various styles, sizes and shapes, as well as plates and trays. Brocton Central School students are participating with custom bowls, in addition to the custom pieces created by Ron Nasca, event organizer and owner of Mudslingers Ceramics Gallery in Fredonia.

Prices vary in increments of $5, with each potter setting the price for their work. Cash, checks, debit and credit cards are all accepted, with a small processing fee for credit card transactions.

This year's event has a new area of focus from previous years, as it aims to also fill the empty bowls of our four-legged friends. Guests are encouraged to bring canned dog or cat food to donate to Lakeshore Humane Society and The Pet Pantry in Dunkirk. Guests who bring a can of pet food receive a raffle ticket for a prize at the event.

For his own custom pieces for sale at Empty Bowls, Nasca has used historic local clay from various sites across the county in recent years, including 200-year-old clay from when the Darwin R. Barker Historical Museum was originally constructed, as well as clay from the Haven and Kenyon Pottery site in Sheridan.

local.title: Measles outbreak defies advances in medicine
local.summary: My medical training didn’t prepare me for this moment. I grew up in Warren County, Pa., but now live in Buffalo and work as a hospitalist, meaning If you become a patient at the hospital and have to stay overnight or are not going straight to surgery, I am often one of the doctors taking […]
local.body:
I grew up in Warren County, Pa., but now live in Buffalo and work as a hospitalist, meaning If you become a patient at the hospital and have to stay overnight or are not going straight to surgery, I am often one of the doctors taking care of you.

I recently went to speak at a conference in Lancaster, Pa., at the center of the current largest U.S. outbreak of measles, which claimed its sixth death this past week. As I prepared for that trip, I found myself pondering how to reduce my exposure.

I worried, not for myself, but for my beloved (and fully vaccinated) toddler and aging parents who love to visit their grandchild. Current vaccine guidance says my childhood vaccines likely protect me, but immunity is not always perfect, and I was headed to a high-risk area. Should I repeat my vaccination?

If you had told me in medical school (11 years ago) that I would have to plan for patients with vaccine-preventable diseases which had previously been almost completely eliminated in the United States, I would not have believed you.

I have previously written about the importance of COVID and flu vaccinations. Now I must discuss the childhood vaccination schedule as well, as people in prominent positions of leadership continue to undermine evidence and diminish the confidence people once had in vaccines.

We see real-time consequences as outbreaks of vaccine-preventable diseases appear across the country. They are not caused by immigrant communities, undocumented or otherwise (as one myth claims), but by American communities where vaccinations have decreased. I was glad to see several Warren-area medical professionals (including my father, a now-retired pediatrician) sign a statement encouraging vaccinations and emphasizing their importance in public health.

Some people have claimed that doctors are not taught about vaccines, which is false. We all experience a pediatrics rotation, learn about diseases vaccines prevent, and study basics of vaccine components. Still, over the past six years I have looked at vaccine inserts and ingredients with much greater scrutiny, to explain them better to people via social media and to understand what my family and I receive. I am grateful for the plethora of vaccine and disease research making that work possible.

Yet my medical training did not anticipate this. So I think about the toddler here and his grandparents in Warren, and how vaccines help us protect ourselves and also protect the vulnerable around us.

local.body: Five months after Buffalo Police Officer Marc Hurst was shot six times while responding to a domestic violence call, he celebrated a moment that once seemed far from certain: marrying his fiancée, Haley."I'm just so thankful, you know, that we are celebrating our marriage on Friday and my family and my fiancée is not mourning the loss of me," Hurst said in an interview earlier this week.Hurst was responding to a call about a violent domestic May 26 near Broadway and Sherman Street when he was shot."One officer shot. Every available to Sherman," a dispatcher could be heard saying over police radio.Hurst was struck six times and rushed to ECMC.One of Hurst's friends in the police department called Haley with the news."I was like, 'You need to tell me what's going on,'" Haley recalled. "And he said that Marc had been shot."At first, she didn't know how serious his injuries were."I was obviously freaking out, like, he's been shot everywhere," she said.Hurst remembers realizing that despite being shot multiple times, he was still breathing and able to think."I just remember, and I believe it's just from the Lord, this overwhelming peace," Hurst said.As he focused on getting out of the house, another thought crossed his mind: his upcoming wedding."I remember being down on the ground and focusing on getting out of the house that we were in, but also being like, 'You know what? She's gonna be really ticked off if I miss this wedding.'"Hurst survived. local.body: New York Assembly Speaker Carl Heastie faces questions about how a political committee under his control spent more than $1 million on sports-related events, including luxury suites and tickets to games involving some of the state's most popular professional sports teams.An investigation by New York Focus found the Democratic Assembly Campaign Committee paid teams, stadiums and sports-related companies more than $1 million since Heastie became Assembly Speaker in 2015. The spending included events involving the New York Yankees, New York Mets, Buffalo Sabres, Madison Square Garden, Barclays Center and UBS Arena.Heastie, a well-known sports fan, attended a number of those events, including a Subway Series game at Citi Field, an NBA playoff matchup at Madison Square Garden and games at Yankee Stadium.The investigation raises questions about whether the events were primarily legitimate political fundraising activities or provided personal benefits to Heastie and other political figures.The Democratic Assembly Campaign Committee's housekeeping account can accept unlimited corporate donations. However, state law restricts how that money can be spent.Housekeeping funds are intended to pay for permanent party headquarters and staff, as well as ordinary party activities that are not specifically intended to promote individual candidates.Spending that money on fundraising for the committee is permitted, and financial disclosure documents frequently listed fundraising as the expense code for the sports-related expenditures.But New York Focus reporter Sam Mellins questioned whether fundraising was always the actual goal, especially considering the photos Heastie posted on social media, posing with sports stars, friends and colleagues."Was that the primary purpose of the events, or was it primarily for the personal benefit of the politicians and the political figures involved? I don't feel 100% confident about that," Mellins said.State law prohibits campaign funds from being spent on purely personal expenses.Mellins said Heastie personally benefited from attending games in luxury suites and box seats, even if there may have been a legitimate political purpose for some of the events.One of the companies that provided significant support to the committee was Buffalo-based Delaware North.The company donated luxury suite packages, including one for a Boston Celtics game Hea

local.title: Community group fighting back after illegal dumping plagues Buffalo
local.summary: Illegal dumping has plagued private and city-owned vacant lots in Buffalo for years, and an abandoned boat now sitting at the Wonder Bread factory shows the problem isn't going away.
local.body: Illegal dumping has plagued private and city-owned vacant lots in Buffalo for years, and an abandoned boat now sitting at the Wonder Bread factory shows the problem isn't going away.I first spoke with Kevin Hayes at the East Side site back in July, after he reached out to tell me about the ongoing issue."Someone left their boat here," Hayes said. "It's been here for two months."He said the situation has worsened since the summer. "The city hasn't taken anything away," Hayes said.The property is owned by Harry Stinson, who also owns the vacant Buffalo Grand Hotel. Hayes said he believes it is Stinson's responsibility to clean the site, but that the city needs to tackle illegal dumping in the neighborhood - both on the streets and on city-owned vacant lots.WATCH: Community group fighting back after illegal dumping plagues BuffaloJust a few blocks away, the city is testing a way to do exactly that. Fencing on Northampton Street is part of an anti-dumping pilot project. It has been in place since July, and the city said the fencing will remain in place with the hope of expanding the project to other sites.Other city-led prevention measures include trap cameras, as first reported by 7 News. A city spokesperson said there are now four active trap cameras and they have plans to activate a further four next week. They did not reveal the location of the cameras. WATCH: Buffalo to deploy trap cameras to crack down on illegal dumping citywideSome community members nearby have also taken matters into their own hands.One dead-end street is surrounded by city-owned vacant lots. The nonprofit Open Buffalo is stewarding the 10-acre property, with plans to turn it into an eco campus. The site was a target for illegal dumping in September."They went in the back and dumped a home - furniture, passport, license and all of those things," said Franchelle Parker, Executive Director at Open Buffalo. Parker and her team have created natural barriers to prevent illegal dumping from happening again."We've had some of our volunteers go through what's called 'CPTD,' crime prevention through environmental design," Parker said.Volunteers have used tree limbs and rocks to create barriers. local.title: Downtown Buffalo businesses show signs of growth as new shops prepare to open
local.summary: After years of downtown businesses closing their doors, signs of a shift are showing, with some local businesses expanding and others preparing to open.
local.body: After years of downtown businesses closing their doors, signs of a shift are showing, with some local businesses expanding and others preparing to open.For customers like Esther Nyakato, the growth is something worth celebrating.Nyakato considers herself a loyal regular at Jack's Corner Cafe, where she says the food, drinks and staff keep her coming back.Jack's Corner Cafe recently reopened at 130 Genesee Street after closing its original location for nearly two weeks to move into a larger space right across the street.For employees, it means more room to serve customers and a more comfortable environment."It's amazing. I like the new space. It's so much more comfortable. We aren't on top of each other," said Zoya Amore, a barista who has worked at the cafe for five years, since it first opened.Amore said the response has been positive, with familiar customers continuing to stop in."The response has been good," she said. "We seem to have our regulars almost every day."Nyakato said the cafe's expansion reflects the support given by the community."That shows how much people love this place and are coming and seeing regulars," she said. "The people I work with also recommended this place." WATCH: Downtown Buffalo businesses show signs of growth as new shops prepare to openAnd Jack's Corner Cafe is not the only business bringing activity downtown.ERTH, a specialty Yemeni coffee shop, is expected to open in the coming weeks at The Hotel @ The Lafayette, adding another coffee option to the downtown area.Meanwhile, a new bookstore called The Walrus Said is preparing to open at 600 Main Street, near Chippewa.The new openings come as small businesses continue to navigate high costs and the challenges of operating in an evolving economic climate.For Nyakato, seeing local businesses grow is important not just for customers, but for the surrounding community."It's important to see that local businesses can flourish with the local people and basically uplift the community. It's something we can keep seeing, hopefully," she said.As more businesses look to establish themselves downtown, their investments could help shape what the next chapter looks like.

local.body:
Listen • 4:11 New York Public News Network reporters Jon Campbell and Samuel King talk about the latest developments at the State Capitol in Albany.

Gov. Kathy Hochul won a resounding victory over her Republican challenger, Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman, in this year’s election.

The governor was able to improve her margin in all 62 counties compared to 2022 — every single one of them.

Attorney General Letitia James and Comptroller Thomas DiNapoli also won their reelection bids.

Republicans were hopeful that their messaging about Hochul and failed leadership by Democrats would counteract the national mood against President Donald Trump and Republicans but that was not the case.

Republicans also suffered losses in the state Legislature. They lost seats on Long Island, in New York City, the Capital Region and other parts of the state, which means the Democrats have regained a two-thirds supermajority in the Senate and will now have the largest majority in party history in the Assembly.

local.title: Mark Cuddy returning as interim artistic director at Geva
local.summary: Cuddy was artistic director for nearly three decades until retiring in 2022.
local.body:
Geva Theatre's former artistic director Mark Cuddy is returning in an interim role, the nonprofit announced Friday.

Cuddy was artistic director for nearly three decades until retiring in 2022. He is coming back to help with the transitional period between the departure next month of artistic director Elizabeth Williamson, and her yet-to-be-named successor.

The Geva Board of Trustees expects to launch a recruitment process for the next artistic director soon.

Cuddy will continue to lead The Classics Company , which he founded last year. In the interim role he will work alongside theater leadership, staff and artists to oversee the remainder of the current season, lead planning for next season, and provide overall artistic leadership during the transition, according to the release.

local.title: Route 20 Ice Cream turns freezers into grocery giveaways
local.summary: The freezers at Route 20 Ice Cream are usually filled with treats. But as the ice cream season winds down, the Orchard Park business is putting that space to a different use: helping families put food on the table.
local.body: The freezers at Route 20 Ice Cream are usually filled with treats. But as the ice cream season winds down, the Orchard Park business is putting that space to a different use: helping families put food on the table.The shop is preparing hundreds of grocery bags as part of its annual Gratitude Groceries giveaway, an effort to provide food to 800 families across two distribution days.Owner Dave Kaiser said the idea formed after his wife, Beth, noticed the shop's freezers were empty during the offseason."Our freezers are empty. Let's get some groceries and do a food giveaway," Kaiser said. The effort is growing in its second year with help from friends Bill and Colleen Loecher, who insisted on splitting the cost of the groceries with the Kaisers. Their contribution allowed them to purchase more food and increase the number of groceries available to families.WATCH: Route 20 Ice Cream turns freezers into grocery giveawaysOrganizers plan to distribute groceries to 400 families on Saturday, November 7, and another 400 families on Tuesday, November 10. Each family will receive three bags: two containing dry goods and one containing frozen items.Kaiser said he and his wife understand that anyone can find themselves in a position where they need a little extra help."We've all been in situations where we need some help," Kaiser said. "And to be able to do this for others is a blessing for us."Gratitude Groceries giveaway details:Saturday, November 7: 3 p.m. to 6 p.m.Tuesday, November 10: 4 p.m. to 7 p.m.Location: 2783 Southwestern Blvd, Orchard Park, NY 14127The goal is to help 800 families through the two giveaways, turning what would otherwise be empty ice cream freezers into an opportunity to give back to the community.

entertainment.title: Hilary Swank's Acting Career Started On A Sitcom Spin-Off Of An '80s Kids Movie
entertainment.summary: Long before "Yellowjackets," Hilary Swank and her mom struggled with homelessness. It finally paid off when Swank landed a guest role in this spin-off.
entertainment.body:
Both the sitcom and the original film are about the Henderson family, who accidentally hit a sasquatch with their car. They subsequently adopt him and name him "Harry."

Swank appeared in the 13th episode of the first season as Chelsea, a friend of the Hendersons' teenage daughter Sarah (Carol-Ann Plante). Chelsea arrives at the Hendersons' house as Sarah's parents George (Bruce Davison) and Nancy (Molly Cheek) are leaving for dinner, leaving Sarah to babysit her younger brother Ernie (Zachary Bostrom). Chelsea convinces Sarah to stop making pies for a bake sale and accompany her to a local pizza joint where their crush works. Despite Chelsea's protests, Sarah brings Ernie with them, leaving Harry alone to ransack the house (and the pies).

ABC While Swank's role on the sitcom was brief, it helped her break through in Hollywood.

Before appearing in "Harry and the Hendersons," the teenage Swank and her mother Judy struggled with homelessness. After Judy separated from Swank's father, she moved her daughter to Los Angeles to help her get into acting. Before finding an apartment, the two were forced to sleep in an Oldsmobile Cutlass Supreme.

She recounted this time in her life to The Wall Street Journal . "When we weren't sleeping in the car, we stayed at the house of a new friend my age whose family had just moved out and were trying to sell their home. We slept on an air mattress."

Swank soon hired agent Bonnie Liedtke to represent her, and she landed her inaugural role in "Harry and the Hendersons." She would appear in shows such as "Growing Pains" and Burt Reynolds' "Evening Shade" before going into films.
